findings.quote: The **nitrogen cycle** moves nitrogen through air, soil, water, and living things. **Nitrogen fixation** changes atmospheric $N_2$ into ammonia, which is often present as ammonium $NH_4^+$ in water or soil. Some bacteria then carry out **nitrification**, which changes ammonium into nitrite and nitrate. Plants take up usable nitrogen compounds, while **denitrification** returns nitrogen gases to the air.
findings.problem: This Core Concept paragraph has four sentences, exceeding the rule that paragraphs contain one to three short sentences.

findings.quote: The **phosphorus cycle** moves phosphorus mainly through rocks, soil, water, and living things. Weathering releases phosphate from rocks. Plants take it up from soil or water, animals get it by feeding, and waste and decay return it. Runoff can carry phosphate into bodies of water, where some may later become part of sediment.
findings.problem: This Core Concept paragraph has four sentences, exceeding the rule that paragraphs contain one to three short sentences.

illustrations.position_quote: In a food web, grass is eaten by rabbits and grasshoppers. Frogs eat grasshoppers. Hawks eat both rabbits and frogs.
illustrations.description: A simple food web with arrows from grass to rabbits and grasshoppers, grasshoppers to frogs, and rabbits and frogs to hawks.
illustrations.why: Seeing the branches makes the alternate food path clear and helps explain why a grasshopper decline affects frogs more directly than hawks.

science-biology#28.quote: Population size can change when organisms are born, die, enter an area, or leave it. Food, water, space, disease, predators, and other conditions can also limit growth.
science-biology#28.note: The lesson now teaches population change, limiting conditions, carrying capacity, competition, predators, and other community interactions.

science-biology#29.quote: Losing a species can change feeding relationships, competition, and other links in a community. The effect depends on the role of that species and on the rest of the food web.
science-biology#29.note: The rewrite now teaches biodiversity loss and its possible consequences for community relationships.

science-biology#30.quote: Human activities can change ecosystems. Common causes include habitat loss, pollution, taking organisms faster than their populations can recover, and changes in climate. An **invasive species** is an introduced species that spreads and causes harm in its new area.
science-biology#30.note: The lesson now covers several major human impacts on ecosystems and defines invasive species.

science-biology#31.quote: **Conservation** protects species, habitats, and natural resources so they can keep supporting life. Actions may include protecting or restoring habitat, reducing pollution, controlling invasive species, limiting harvest so populations can replace what is taken, and monitoring populations.
science-biology#31.note: The rewrite now teaches species and resource conservation actions and connects environmental management to the cause of damage.
